To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the tracheolar diameter in insects is optimized for diffusion of oxygen at low partial pressures, and (ii) the tracheoles are optimized to minimize diffusive losses at the transition between free molecular and continuum regimes of diffusion.
The diffusion of oxygen through insect tracheoles is limited by the transition regime, which occurs at tracheole diameters of about 0.2 μm.

(a) the transition regime of diffusion is a critical parameter in determining the structure of the tracheolar system in insects; (b) the transition regime is reached when the effective tracheal diameter is approximately equal to the mean free path; (c) the transition regime occurs in insects when the effective diameter is approximately 0.5μm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure of the respiratory system in insects.
the diffusion of oxygen molecules through the tracheolar system of an insect.
the development of a mathematical model of oxygen transport through insect tracheoles, and the application of this model to the problem of the structure of the tracheolar system in insects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the insect tracheoles are not the smallest possible tubes for diffusion, but are the smallest tubes which are still effective in the transition regime, where the mean free path is comparable to the effective tracheal diameter.
in the insect respiratory system, the tracheoles are arranged to provide the greatest possible surface area for the diffusion of gases and to minimize the diffusion distance.
, as the diameter of the tracheole is reduced, the oxygen diffusion rate increases, until it reaches a maximum at the transition regime diameter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tracheolar system of the insect is designed for maximum efficiency in diffusion of oxygen.
the insect tracheal system is optimized for diffusion of oxygen at low pressures, and that this optimization is accomplished by the development of a branching pathway of small diameter tracheoles.
we have shown how the structure of the tracheolar system can be related to its function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when designing a respiratory system, it is not sufficient to optimize the system for a single mode of transport (e.g. diffusion).

, when the tracheolar diameter approaches the size of a single oxygen molecule, the diffusion process is no longer described by Fick's law, and the effective diffusion coefficient becomes a function of the tracheolar radius.
there is an optimal tracheolar diameter that maximizes the rate of oxygen diffusion along a tracheole, and that this diameter is approximately equal to the mean free path.
